Square Sieve

Number TheoryDivisibilityRiemann Hypothesis
Game: Flip the colours of numbers again and again, then see which ones end up red.
How to play: Press the step button: it flips every number in the times table of its step number. Keep pressing until the steps run out.
Look for the math

Flipping a switch twice puts it back, so each number's final colour depends only on whether the number of flips is odd or even.

Divisors come in pairs

Number m is flipped on step k exactly when k divides m. So the number of flips is the number of divisors of m. Divisors pair up as m = a × b, and the flips from steps a and b cancel. The only divisor without a partner is a = b, which happens only when m = a².

The red numbers are the squares

So after all N steps exactly 1, 4, 9, 16, … are red. The logic test confirmed this for every N from 5 to 250, and that a number never changes after its own step. The applet's flipping rule (step m touches indexes m, 2m, 3m, …) is the same as the one tested. This is also the locker puzzle: students open and close lockers, and only the perfect-square lockers end open.

A link to the Riemann Hypothesis

This sieve counts divisors, and the divisor-counting function is one of the sums behind the zeta function, which is what the Riemann Hypothesis is about. How many divisors a number has, on average, is tied to how regular the primes are.

Set N to 250 and press "Do all the steps". Count the red numbers: how many squares are there up to 250?
